tldr: GEA introduces a group-centric evolutionary paradigm for open-ended self-improvement, enabling explicit experience sharing among agents to consolidate exploratory diversity into sustained progress, significantly outperforming existing tree-structured self-evolving methods on coding benchmarks.
contributions: Proposes Group-Evolving Agents (GEA), a new paradigm treating a group of agents as the fundamental evolutionary unit with explicit intra-group experience sharing and reuse.
Overcomes the inefficient utilization of exploratory diversity caused by isolated branches in existing tree-structured evolution.
Demonstrates that GEA matches or exceeds state-of-the-art human-designed frameworks without human intervention.
Shows consistent transferability across different coding models (GPT and Claude-series) and greater robustness to framework-level perturbations.
methods: GEA maintains an archive of all discovered agents. At each iteration, it selects a parent group of K agents using a Performance-Novelty criterion balancing task performance with evolutionary diversity measured via cosine distance on task-success vectors. The parent group then jointly produces an offspring group through open-ended group evolution, where each agent collects its own evolutionary traces (applied patches, predicted task patches, execution logs, outcome logs), aggregates them into a shared pool across the group, and uses a reflection module to generate evolution directives followed by an evolution module producing framework-level patches. Agents that compile successfully and exhibit basic coding functionality are added to the archive.
results: On SWE-bench Verified, GEA achieved 71.0% compared to 56.7% for the DGM baseline (under matched evolved agent counts), and 71.0% vs. 71.8% for the top human-designed framework (OpenHands + GPT-5). On Polyglot, GEA achieved 88.3% vs. 68.3% for DGM and 88.3% vs. 52.0% for Aider + GPT-5. GEA fixes framework-level bugs in 1.4 iterations on average versus 5 for self-evolving methods. GEA reached 88.3% on Polyglot in just 4 iterations with 8,677 lines of code added, and 71.0% on SWE-bench Verified in 8 iterations with 9,663 lines added.
limitations: Staged evaluation strategy was adopted due to substantial cost of evaluating every evolved agent on full benchmarks, which may not capture full performance.

Different evolutionary patterns were observed between benchmarks (Polyglot requiring single-file edits vs. SWE-bench requiring multi-file coordination), suggesting task complexity affects patch characteristics and convergence speed.
Computational budget constraints required using different model configurations across iterations (Claude Haiku 4.5 for first iterations, Claude Sonnet 4.5 for final iterations).
